receipts.first_text_witness: You're pulling into a Costco parking lot on a Saturday afternoon and you watch a brand new pickup truck back into the spot next to yours. Crew cab, blacked out grill, factory fresh paint, the kind of chrome that hurts your eyes a little in direct sunlight. A guy steps out. He's wearing the polo shirt with the embroidered logo from the regional HVAC company he works for. Lunchbox on the passenger seat, there's a kids car seat in the back. He walks around to the bed, unlatches the tailgate, and loads in one case
receipts.last_text_witness: a truck, if you tow, if you haul, if you run a business out of the bed, if you live somewhere where four-wheel drive is genuinely the difference between getting to work and not getting there, then buy the truck with clear eyes, knowing the real cost. But, if you don't, the bravest financial decision you can make in 2026 isn't buying the truck. It's looking at the math, looking at the salesman, looking at the chrome, and saying, "No, thanks. I'll keep my retirement."

primary_source_receipts.finding: March 2026 full-size pickup mean transaction price was $65,964; February was $66,141. Luxury full-size pickups are a separate category. The table excludes applied consumer incentives.
primary_source_receipts.methodology: This is a mean, not a median, MSRP or out-the-door quote. The March report was in an April 2026 release file and contemporaneous coverage, before upload; its exact release day was not recovered. A full-year 2026 average was not yet observable.

primary_source_receipts.finding: U.S. 2024 pretax household money-income median was $83,730. Table A-2 reports 10.1% at $150K–$199,999 and 16.0% at $200K or more, totaling 26.1% at $150K or more.
primary_source_receipts.methodology: Calendar 2024 income collected in the 2025 CPS ASEC; U.S. households, not individuals or truck purchasers. Money income is pretax and is not take-home pay. No 2026 income estimate is inferred.

primary_source_receipts.finding: In Q4 2025, 20.3% of financed new purchases had monthly payments of at least $1,000. Mean term was 69.6 months and APR 6.7%.
primary_source_receipts.methodology: The relevant denominator is financed new purchases in the transaction sample. Cash purchases and leases cannot silently enter it; dollar thresholds include exactly $1,000.

primary_source_receipts.finding: In Q1 2026, 43% of new loans involving negative-equity trade-ins extended to 84 months. All-new-vehicle mean term was 70.3 months and APR 6.9%.
primary_source_receipts.methodology: This covers new vehicles with negative-equity trade-ins, not trucks alone. Direct Python retrieval returned HTTP403; the original page was accessible through web extraction/search. Different samples and quarters must not be merged.

primary_source_receipts.finding: Nearly 30% of new financed vehicles had 73–84-month terms in Q4 2025. The mean new rate was 6.37%, versus 11.26% for used vehicles.
primary_source_receipts.methodology: Original institutional release dated March 5, 2026. All-new financing term shares are not truck-specific; rate differences from Edmunds are not automatically errors.

primary_source_receipts.finding: Purchase affordability requires considering financing, insurance, fuel, maintenance and other ownership costs alongside the household budget.
primary_source_receipts.methodology: Pre-upload review date displayed, but no upload-day HTML capture. This guidance gives no universal salary or 20/4/10 requirement.

primary_source_receipts.finding: Compare APR, interest rate, term, amount financed and total cost rather than the payment alone.
primary_source_receipts.methodology: Pre-upload review date displayed. APR can include credit costs beyond note interest; a fee-free monthly model does not certify an actual lender offer.

primary_source_receipts.finding: Depreciation and loan amortization jointly determine vehicle equity; rolling negative equity into a replacement loan raises its principal.
primary_source_receipts.methodology: Original June 2024 PDF search extraction reviewed. This does not verify a universal instantaneous 20% truck loss or a particular residual value.

primary_source_receipts.finding: For selected 2025 half-ton crew-cab models, modeled cost was $14,781 annually at 15K miles, including depreciation and finance charges. Insurance was $1,699 annually, license/registration/taxes $1,098, and maintenance/repair/tires 11.36 cents per mile.
primary_source_receipts.methodology: Five selected top-selling models per category and a five-year cost framework; this is not a quote for one $50K truck or a seven-year cash budget. Loan principal is not an additional expense alongside depreciation. September 2026 findings were not used.

primary_source_receipts.finding: Current 2026 XLT starting MSRP is $44,695 before $2,795 destination and other fees. The model adds to the base model and offers multiple cab, engine and bed configurations.
primary_source_receipts.methodology: Current page, not an archived May quote. Current builder lists XL below XLT; Ford pages differ on the XL starting configuration. Do not use current prices to declare an exact historical MSRP false.

primary_source_receipts.finding: Current manufacturer 2026 page lists WT at $37,200 and LT at $48,200 starting. LT is not the lowest WT trim.
primary_source_receipts.methodology: Main URL now defaults to 2027; the explicit previous-year link was followed. Search index showed $47,900 while live page showed $48,200. Exact May price, destination basis and configuration remain unverified.

primary_source_receipts.finding: The original manufacturer fleet guide distinguishes Tradesman and Big Horn and lists different equipment groups. It does not independently certify the transcript’s exact historical $47,500 configuration.
primary_source_receipts.methodology: Original manufacturer search extraction and current Ram page reviewed. Exact issue date and historical price basis remain unverified; no equal towing or payload capacity is inferred.

primary_source_receipts.finding: NVES studies new U.S. car and light-truck owners. The claimed original truck-usage tables and 250K truck-specific sample were not recovered.
primary_source_receipts.methodology: Current institutional context only. Field dates, weighting, questions and the quoted 75/70/35/90 and 63/32/87 percentages remain unavailable. F-150 owners cannot stand for all truck owners.

primary_source_receipts.finding: Q1 2026 median usual weekly earnings for full-time wage and salary workers were $1,235 before taxes and other deductions.
primary_source_receipts.methodology: Age16+ full-time wage/salary workers in the CPS; individual gross earnings are not household income or measured median take-home pay. Taxes and deductions are missing.

primary_source_receipts.finding: Stocks fluctuate and losses are possible. A future 8% return is not guaranteed.
primary_source_receipts.methodology: Current investor guidance with no recovered historical publication date. It does not establish a historical S&P500 average or a retirement outcome.

primary_source_receipts.finding: The index publisher distinguishes price, net total and total returns across different annualized windows. Its current snapshot does not verify the video’s undefined historical 8% average.
primary_source_receipts.methodology: Later/current index snapshot is explicitly retrospective. No post-upload market return is used as evidence the creator could have known it. Period, dividends, fees and return convention remain essential.

calculation_receipts.assumptions: Same channel, format and frozen 2026-09-11 snapshot; ages >=7 days; peer age 0.5–2 times target; nearest absolute age distance then Video_ID; ten peers and first-five sensitivity. STRONG >=2; WEAK <0.5; otherwise TYPICAL. Four-decimal ages preserved; lifetime rate is not current velocity or a causal estimate.

target.Title: Who Can Actually Afford a $50K Truck in 2026?

calculation_receipts.method: Monthly loan payment, total interest and year-one balance
calculation_receipts.assumptions: Monthly fully amortizing loan, first payment after one month, no financed fees, taxes, balloon, daily-interest timing or prepayment. APR may differ from note interest when fees exist. Resale is creator assumption, not verified market value.

Creator mileage, economy and pump price are scenario inputs; insurance and maintenance are not actual quotes. Quoted items sum1395, round1400. Loan principal is a cash outflow and asset-equity transfer, not an expense to add again to depreciation. No seven-year fixed operating-cost forecast.

calculation_receipts.method: Garcia household residual and commute sensitivity
calculation_receipts.assumptions: Fictional budget; $5,600 take-home is assumed, not a tax estimate. 260 workdays is an analyst sensitivity, not observed employment. CRV and other household expenses are omitted; the stated commute is 76 miles/day.

Same 7% note rate assumed at four-year term; TOTAL transportation costs, not loan payment alone, limited to10% gross. No other household vehicle, debt or financed fees. This heuristic is not a universal affordability or lender eligibility rule.

End-of-month contributions. Quoted1.04M reproduces nominal8%/12 convention; effective annual8% convention yields985985.41. Constant return assumption, not forecast. Taxes, fund fees and inflation omitted. Continuous30-year savings must be established separately from an84-month loan.

Own sensitivity examples, not creator predictions. Only7 years of contributions then23years growth; alternatively continuous30year contributions at6% or10%. Own3% inflation yields429805.85 in initial-year purchasing power; no inflation forecast or guaranteed retirement age.
Census2024 pretax household money-income distribution, not2026 purchaser distribution or individual salaries. Two conflicting depreciation scenarios not blended.

Own reconciliation using creator later31K year-five residual, not a verified resale quote. Equal sums prove how to avoid principal/depreciation double count. Operating costs would be added once on either side. No terminal loan balance is treated as sale equity.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
$50,000 used to buy you a really
nice truck. Today $50,000 barely gets
you a base model with the door panels
and the wheels included.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: Undated price-history rhetoric is not a comparable trim or real-dollar series. A $50K universal minimum for new full-size pickups is not demonstrated.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
average transaction price for a new
full-size pickup in 2026 is about
$66,000.
$66,000, that's the average. That's what
the typical buyer is actually driving
off the lot in.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: About $66K agrees with the March 2026 mean of $65,964. A mean is not the typical buyer’s median, an out-the-door quote or a completed 2026 annual average. The source excludes applied consumer incentives.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
A
base Ford F-150 XLT, which is the most
popular trim, has an MSRP
right around $48,500.
A Chevy Silverado LT around $47,900.
A Ram 1500 Big Horn, roughly $47,500.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: XLT, LT and Big Horn are not the respective lowest XL, WT and Tradesman trims. The exact historical prices and XLT popularity rank remain unverified. Cab, bed, drivetrain, engine and destination basis are missing; current prices cannot prove May quotations wrong.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
By the time you add a couple of options,
taxes, doc fees, and whatever creative
line item the dealership invents that
week, you've crossed $50,000 without
even ordering leather seats.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: Options, taxes and fees can raise an out-the-door price above $50K, but the state, configuration and negotiated deal matter. The later $50K loan example does not itemize those costs.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
median household income in
America right now is about $84,000
a year pre-tax. That means we are asking
the average American household to spend
roughly 60%
of their entire pre-tax annual income on
one vehicle.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: $84K reasonably rounds the 2024 CPS household median of $83,730 released September 2025. This was an available estimate, not observed 2026 income. $50K/$84K=59.52%; using $83,730 gives 59.72%. Household median is not individual mean income.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
will be worth about half of what they
paid for it within 5 years.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: No model, mileage, condition or residual-value source establishes 50% retention. Later $10K plus $9K cumulative depreciation implies $31K remaining, or 62% retention, contradicting the earlier assumption.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
It's the
floor. It's the lowest rung on a ladder
where the average rung is $66,000,
and the top rung, the Raptor R you see
on TikTok, is $113,000.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: The $50K floor and $113K Raptor R depend on missing configurations and historical price receipts. Selected middle trims do not establish the lowest full-size price. No equal towing or payload comparison is asserted here.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
same as a 4-year
degree.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: The degree comparison lacks tuition versus attendance, public versus private, residency and period definitions. Parents’ first house and sports cars from 20 years ago are also undated rhetorical comparisons.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
average new auto loan in America right
now stretches almost 69 months. That's 5
and 1/2 years, but for trucks
specifically nearly 30% of new vehicle
loans are now between 73 and 84 months.
That's 6 to 7 years.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: Edmunds Q4 mean term was 69.6 months (5.8 years); Q1 was 70.3. Experian’s nearly 30% at 73–84 months describes new financed vehicles, not trucks specifically. Even 69 months is 5.75 years, not 5.5.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
for buyers
rolling over negative equity from their
last truck, 43% of those loans get
stretched to the full 84 months.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: 43% is verified for Q1 2026 new loans involving negative-equity trade-ins across vehicles, not a truck-only subset. The earlier Q4 figure differs by period and need not contradict it.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
loses 20% of its value the
second you drive it off the lot.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: Instantaneous 20% depreciation is unverified for this unspecified truck. The script later applies 20% after one year. Depreciation risk is real, but its size and timing require a vehicle-specific resale assumption.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
You buy a $50,000
truck. You put $0 down because you don't
have 10 grand sitting around. And
neither does anyone else. We'll be
generous and say you got a 7% interest

average.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: Zero down and 7% are explicit hypothetical inputs. 7% is close to Edmunds Q1 6.9%, not a universal offer; Experian Q4 6.37% covers a different sample. The rhetorical claim that nobody has $10K cash is unsupported. Note interest, APR and financed fees must be distinguished.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
You stretch it over 84 months
to make the payment feel manageable.
Your monthly payment is $754.85.
Sounds reasonable, right? Under $800 a
month, you can do that. Now, here's the
magic trick revealed. Over the life of
that loan, you will pay $63,407
for a truck that cost $50,000. That's
$13,407
in interest.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: Standard monthly amortization gives $754.634, $63,389.256 total and $13,389.256 interest. The quoted $754.85/$63,407/$13,407 differ by $0.216 monthly and about $17.74 total, a minor precision error. $754.85×84=$63,407.40; no additional fees explain the exact quoted payment.
calculation_receipts: Monthly loan payment, total interest and year-one balance

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:

financial_claim_locations.assessment: After 12 monthly payments, balance is $44,262.638, not $45,700. With assumed $40K resale, negative equity is $4,262.638, not $5,700. Principal repaid is $5,737.362. Resale itself remains conditional.
calculation_receipts: Monthly loan payment, total interest and year-one balance

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
In the fourth
quarter of 20 25, 20.3%

financial_claim_locations.assessment: 20.3% describes financed new purchases, not all new purchases or all buyers. The source threshold is at least $1,000, not strictly above $1,000. Cash transactions and leases cannot silently enter that denominator.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
a third of the
median full-time workers take-home pay
just for the privilege of getting to and
from their job.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: $1,000 as one-third implies $3,000 monthly net pay. BLS reports $1,235 median gross weekly earnings, about $5,351.67 monthly. Taxes, filing status and deductions are needed; gross earnings do not verify a national median take-home figure.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
top
15% of American earners. The other 85%
are at the used lot down the street
financing a 2019 Silverado at 14%
interest because the new market has
quietly stopped including them.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: No buyer-income distribution verifies a blanket top-15% purchaser claim. Individual and household denominators switch. The later statement that most truck buyers earn $60K–$100K conflicts with this framing. A 14% used APR is possible, not a universal observed mean.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
being approved, I cannot
stress this enough, is not the same as
being able to afford it.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: Loan approval and household residual-income affordability are different. Claims about banks expecting ramen or skipped dentistry are rhetoric, not observed underwriting requirements.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
Insurance
on a new $50,000 truck, about 185 a
month. That's just for the privilege of
being allowed to drive it. Fuel. A
full-size pickup gets about 18 miles per
gallon combined. 15,000 miles a year at
four bucks a gallon, which in 2026 is
275 a month. Maintenance, oil changes,
the inevitable brake job, 90 a month if
you don't think about it too hard.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: $185 insurance, 18 mpg, $4 gasoline, 15K miles and $90 maintenance are assumptions, not a VIN-specific quote. Fuel computes to $277.78/month, close to $275. AAA’s model differs; its insurance and maintenance averages do not establish this buyer’s bill.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
Tires. Truck tires are not regular
tires. A full set runs 800 to 1,600
installed, and you'll need them around
50,000 miles, which sounds far away
until you remember that's 3 years.
Specialty tires on a Tremor or a
Trailboss, up to 3 grand a set.
Registration and taxes, another 90 a
month depending on your state.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: Tire prices of $800–$1,600 or $3K and a 50K-mile life lack size, brand and installation receipts. 50K miles at 15K annually lasts 3.33 years. $90 registration/taxes is near AAA’s annual modeled amount, but state and upfront-versus-recurring treatment are unspecified.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
Your $50,000 truck loses about 10 grand
of value in year one alone. Another 9
grand by year five. That's value
evaporating off the hood while you
sleep.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: $10K year-one plus another $9K by year five implies $31K residual and 38% cumulative loss, versus the earlier 50% loss. Neither is verified for a specific truck. Do not assume the additional $9K occurs every year.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
Add it all up. Loan payment 755,
insurance 185, fuel 275, maintenance and
tires 90, registration 90. Total $1,400
a month. Every month for 7 years to own
this thing.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: Quoted cash-flow items sum to $1,395 and reasonably round to $1,400. Formula payment and exact fuel give $1,397.412. This is a cash budget, not a complete economic TCO calculation. Financing ends after month 84 and operating costs vary. Adding depreciation to full principal installments double-counts capital cost.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
Meet the Garcias. Both work. Combined
income 90,000 a year, which puts them
above the median. They have two kids.
Carlos works for a mid-size logistics
company. Maria is an elementary school
teacher. They live in a three-bedroom
rental in a suburb where every other
driveway has a pickup in it. Last year,
Carlos bought the $50,000 truck.
84-month loan, zero down. Salesman said
he was approved. Payment is 755.
Here's what their Tuesday looks like
now. Carlos leaves for work at 6:00. He
drives the truck 38 miles each way.
Mostly highway alone. The bed is empty.
It is always empty. Maria takes the kids
to school in their 2014
Honda CRV, which has 140,000 miles and a
check engine light that comes on
whenever it rains. After taxes, the
Garcias take home about 5,600 a month.
Rent is 1850. Uh child care for the
youngest is 1,200. Uh groceries 800,
utilities 350. The truck, all in with
insurance and gas, is 1,400. That leaves
them exactly $0 before they've bought a
single thing they didn't have to buy. No
clothes for the kids, no dentist, no
date night, no savings, no 401k.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: The fictional budget sums exactly: $1,850+$1,200+$800+$350+$1,400=$5,600. Net pay is an assumption, not a verified tax result. CRV expenses, healthcare and other debts are omitted. A 76-mile workday over 260 days already totals 19,760 miles; at 18 mpg/$4, fuel is $365.93 monthly before errands. The transmission failure is a narrative assumption.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
There is this
ongoing study from Strategic Vision that
has surveyed over 250,000
truck owners about how they actually use
their trucks. And here's what they
found. 75% of truck owners tow once a
year or less. Almost 70% go off-road
once a year or less. 35% of truck owners
put something in the bed once a year or
less. Roughly 90% never use their truck
for any kind of work. The Ford F-150
study specifically found that 63% of
owners rarely or never tow, 32% rarely
or never haul anything, and 87%
frequently use the truck for shopping
and errands.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: The original 250K truck-owner sample, field dates, weighting and questions were not recovered. None of the 75/70/35/90% or F-150 63/32/87% pairs is independently verified. Rarely/never is not identical to once per year or less. F-150 owners are not all truck owners, and errands and work can overlap.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote: Dave is just the average truck owner.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: Dave and the unused kayak are fictional illustrations. They do not establish an average truck owner or a causal identity motive.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
Most
people clicked away during the loan
math, which honestly proves the whole
point of the video. The people who most
need to see the next number are the ones
who already left.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: No retention or first-party analytics supports most viewers having left during the math. This is a persistence appeal, not an observed audience result.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
instead of buying
the $50,000 truck, you bought a $20,000
used car, like a 5-year-old Toyota
Camry, boring, reliable, the kind of car
your dentist drives. The total monthly
cost of that Camry, including the loan,
insurance, gas, maintenance, all of it,
would be about $700 a month versus the
$1,400
a month for the truck. That is a
difference of $700 every single month.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: The $20K five-year-old Camry and $700 total monthly cost lack APR, term, down payment, mileage and resale inputs. $1,400−$700=$700 is correct conditionally. Loans end and vehicles need replacement over 30 years; no equal towing or payload claim is made.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
historically returns about
8% annually over the long run.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: The 8% historical claim omits its period, dividends, nominal/real basis and arithmetic/geometric definition. Treat 8% as a modeling assumption, not a verified mean for all windows or a guaranteed return.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
If you
invested $700 a month for 30 years, you
would end up with approximately 1.04
million dollars, 1 million dollars.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: $700 at each month-end for 360 months at 8%/12 gives $1,043,251.614 nominal before taxes, fees and inflation, including $252K contributions. Converting an effective annual 8% to a monthly rate gives $985,985.411. Saving for only seven years and then growing to year 30 gives $491,139.834 in an analyst sensitivity case.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
That
is literally a retirement. That is the
difference between retiring at 65 and
retiring at 75. That is the difference
between leaving your kids something and
leaving them nothing. That is the
difference between dying with options
and dying with bills, all because in
your 30s, you decided you wanted the
truck.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: Retiring at 65 rather than 75, inheritance and certainty of retirement cannot follow without age, other assets, Social Security, spending, longevity, tax and inflation assumptions. No 4% withdrawal rule appears in the transcript. A constant market path and a 30-year cost gap are not established.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
The compounding
opportunity cost of every dollar you
spent on that truck is the actual price,
financial_claim_locations.assessment: Future opportunity cost is a useful separate counterfactual, not another cash price to add on top of purchase and loan payments. Down payment, installments, resale and terminal investment wealth must reconcile over one horizon. A 30-year replacement strategy is missing.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
Nobody at Fidelity is
buying a yacht because you open an index
fund. The whole financial structure of
America is set up to gently nudge you
toward the truck because the truck is
profitable for everyone except you. The
dealer makes the margin, the bank makes
the interest, the insurance company
makes the premiums, the gas station
makes the fill-ups, the manufacturer
makes the markup. The only person in
that entire chain who loses money on the
deal is you.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: Absolute claims that nobody profits from investing and only the buyer loses overlook fund fees, transportation utility and business use. These are incentive arguments, not proof that every purchase destroys buyer welfare; no Fidelity pricing audit is implied.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
Under traditional financial wisdom, the
20/4/10
rule, which says you should put 20%
down, finance for no more than 4 years,
and keep total transportation costs
under 10% of your gross income, the
answer is this. You need to make
approximately $150,000
a year.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: Under the script’s TOTAL transportation ≤10% of gross rule, a $40K/7%/48-month payment of $957.85 plus $185+$275+$90+$90 requires $191,741.97 annual gross income. Exact fuel raises this to $192,075.31. At $150K gross, the $1,250 monthly allowance leaves only $292.15 after financing. The heuristic is not a universal rule.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
You need to have $10,000 in cash
for a down payment. You need to be able
to absorb a monthly payment closer to
$950 on a 4-year loan, not the $755
on the 7-year loan that the salesman is
going to push you toward.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: 20% of $50K is $10K; financing the remaining $40K for 48 months at 7% gives $957.85, reasonably near $950. Taxes/fees and the down payment’s investment opportunity cost are excluded; the same APR across terms is assumed.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
Roughly the
top 15% of American household earners,
not the top 1%, not the rich, but
solidly upper-middle class to wealthy
households.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: CPS 2024 table A-2 places 26.1% of households at $150K or more (10.1% plus 16.0%), not 15%. An individual-earner percentile cannot replace a household one. This income alone proves neither necessary nor sufficient affordability.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
The
people buying the most trucks are
middle-class households making $60,000
to $100,000 a year. The Garcias, the
Daves, they are doing it by stretching
loan terms, putting nothing down, and
quietly accepting that 30% of their
take-home pay will go to their truck for
the next 7 years.
financial_claim_locations.assessment: The claim that most truck purchasers earn $60K–$100K lacks a purchaser-distribution source and conflicts with the earlier blanket top-15% framing. Garcia truck cost is 25% of $5,600 take-home, not 30%; another household might differ. Geography, debt and assets remain necessary.

financial_claim_locations.original_quote:
Add up the loan, the
